question: The geopolitical landscape in northern Europe has changed significantly, with Russia’s aggressive actions and Sweden and Finland’s NATO membership highlighting the critical need for improved infrastructure, particularly east-west connections. No other area in Europe shows such a pronounced lack of connections in the Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T) as northern Europe.

This deficiency is particularly evident in Sweden, where a stretch of nearly 1 000 kilometres from central to northern parts of the country contains just a single east-west connection in the TEN-T network. Given these circumstances: 1.

How is the Commission planning to address the significant infrastructure gaps in northern Europe, particularly the lack of east-west connections, in the light of the changed security situation and enhanced EU security cooperation, in which Sweden and Finland play an important geopolitical role?

How will the Commission help facilitate the integration of strategically important current and future routes, such as those connecting Sweden, Norway and Finland, into the military mobility map to enhance both civil and military preparedness in the region, and ensure co-financing opportunities through the Connecting Europe Facility for these critical infrastructure projects?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.1.2025) In the 2021-2027 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), a budget of EUR 1.69 billion was allocated to co-fund dual-use transport infrastructure through the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF)1.

Following Russia’s aggression against Ukraine in February 2022, the Commission decided to significantly reinforce the support to dual-use transport infrastructure for military mobility by frontloading the available budget. In total, during the current MFF, CEF awarded co-funding worth EUR 1.75 billion to 95 projects in 21 Member States.
All projects selected under the military mobility envelope of the CEF contribute to improve military mobility. In line with the Military Mobility Action Plan 2.

02, the Commission and the European External Action Service took swift action to identify, together with the Member States, priority military mobility corridors for large-scale movements of forces and military materiel at short notice, including in northern Europe (Sweden and Finland).

This work also included the identification of gaps on those priority corridors, including an estimation of the costs to mitigate these gaps, which will help to better guide and prioritise future investments to build a coherent military mobility network.
1 Regulation (EU) 2021/1153 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 July 2021 establishing the
